source_user: A multi-GPU job hangs during collective initialization. Provide a diagnosis plan. Scenario variant 126: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: record ranks and environment; verify process-group rendezvous; inspect topology and GPU visibility; run a minimal all-reduce; test interface selection and timeout; compare single-node and reduced-world runs.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: the framework, NCCL and driver versions, launcher, host count, rank/world-size mapping, GPU model, topology, fabric, interface names, container permissions, rendezvous address, and timeout are unknown. Record them rather than inferring platform facts. Treat “hang” as an observed lack of progress; first identify the last completed phase for every rank and preserve synchronized logs from a failing run and a known-good run.

Prioritized diagnosis and measurements: capture per-rank timestamps for process start, rendezvous join, communicator creation, device selection, each initialization barrier, and the first collective; include PID, hostname, local/global rank, world size, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, selected backend, NCCL debug output, endpoint, interface, and exit/timeout status. Verify that exactly the expected ranks start once, all use identical world size/rendezvous settings, every rank reaches the same call, and the rendezvous port is reachable in both directions. Check GPU visibility, exclusive ownership, rank-to-device mapping, peer access, PCIe/NVLink topology, host clocks, container devices, firewall rules, and NIC/interface routing. Measure connection establishment and collective elapsed time in milliseconds, and collect GPU error state, transport/interface selection, and network counters.

Falsifiable hypothesis: a rank-specific rendezvous or transport-path failure prevents one rank from entering communicator initialization, so the remaining ranks wait indefinitely. It predicts that the failing run will show one missing/late rank or a transport error, while a minimal test with the same ranks and explicit timeout will fail on the same host/interface; forcing a verified interface or correcting rendezvous configuration will make the test complete without changing the model workload. An alternative is an invalid GPU mapping/topology path, which should instead reproduce in a local peer-access or single-node test.

Controlled experiment: use a fixed launcher, image, environment, small deterministic tensor, and a finite timeout (for example, 60 s, not an unlimited wait). Run repeated trials in this order: one node/2 ranks, one node/full local world, a reduced multi-node world, then full world. For each trial compare default interface selection with one explicitly verified interface, and compare the original rank mapping with a known-good mapping; change one factor at a time. Run a minimal all-reduce after communicator creation and record per-rank success, error, and latency. Also run a rendezvous-only check and, where safe, a topology/peer test. Do not conclude from one successful retry; require repeated successes and identical rank logs.

Mitigations and limits: fix rank/world-size or rendezvous configuration, use a reachable interface and documented timeout, remove stale processes, and correct device mapping before changing performance settings. Keep a bounded timeout and fail the job with diagnostics rather than retrying indefinitely. Roll back any interface, topology, or launcher change if the minimal test remains flaky, causes new transport errors, changes the intended network path, or the full job fails correctness. Do not disable safety checks or hide errors; production adoption requires repeated controlled passes, all-rank agreement, and application-level correctness validation. Confounders include unrelated rank crashes, port collisions, firewall/DNS differences, stale processes, version/driver mismatches, link flaps, oversubscription, and a timeout that is shorter than legitimate startup.
risks: platform-specific rendezvous and transport behavior is unverified
minimal fixed tests may not represent full application initialization
interface or timeout changes can mask rather than resolve a rank failure
evidence_required: timestamped logs from every rank and rendezvous/transport diagnostics
repeated fixed-input single-node, reduced-world, and full-world comparisons
topology/interface telemetry plus all-reduce and application correctness checks

Check GPU visibility, exclusive ownership, rank-to-device mapping, peer access, PCIe/NVLink topology, host clocks, container devices, firewall rules, and NIC/interface routing. Measure connection establishment and collective elapsed time in milliseconds, and collect GPU error state, transport/interface selection, and network counters.

Falsifiable hypothesis: a rank-specific rendezvous or transport-path failure prevents one rank from entering communicator initialization, so the remaining ranks wait indefinitely. It predicts that the failing run will show one missing/late rank or a transport error, while a minimal test with the same ranks and explicit timeout will fail on the same host/interface; forcing a verified interface or correcting rendezvous configuration will make the test complete without changing the model workload. An alternative is an invalid GPU mapping/topology path, which should instead reproduce in a local peer-access or single-node test.

Controlled experiment: use a fixed launcher, image, environment, small deterministic tensor, and a finite timeout (for example, 60 s, not an unlimited wait). Run repeated trials in this order: one node/2 ranks, one node/full local world, a reduced multi-node world, then full world. For each trial compare default interface selection with one explicitly verified interface, and compare the original rank mapping with a known-good mapping; change one factor at a time. Run a minimal all-reduce after communicator creation and record per-rank success, error, and latency. Also run a rendezvous-only check and, where safe, a topology/peer test. Do not conclude from one successful retry; require repeated successes and identical rank logs.

Mitigations and limits: fix rank/world-size or rendezvous configuration, use a reachable interface and documented timeout, remove stale processes, and correct device mapping before changing performance settings. Keep a bounded timeout and fail the job with diagnostics rather than retrying indefinitely. Roll back any interface, topology, or launcher change if the minimal test remains flaky, causes new transport errors, changes the intended network path, or the full job fails correctness. Do not disable safety checks or hide errors; production adoption requires repeated controlled passes, all-rank agreement, and application-level correctness validation. Confounders include unrelated rank crashes, port collisions, firewall/DNS differences, stale processes, version/driver mismatches, link flaps, oversubscription, and a timeout that is shorter than legitimate startup.
